Flagship: Model United Nations
Model UN is Country Day's standout competitive academic club by the volume and consistency of its public results. The
school's news archive documents repeat participation at university-hosted conferences with sizeable delegations and
individual awards. At the Model United Nations Chapel Hill (MUNCH) conference on March 1, 2025, seventeen students
represented Country Day and six earned awards, including four Outstanding Delegate honors. A separate Virginia
conference produced a Best Delegate award and a verbal commendation, and the program has also competed at a
conference hosted at Duke University. The club is described as predominantly student-led, with both Middle School and
Upper School delegations active. [Sources: charlottecountryday.org school news — MUNCH; charlottecountryday.org
school news — Virginia MUN; charlottecountryday.org school news — Duke MUN; charlottecountryday.org school news
— Middle School MUN]
Committees students have served on include the United Nations Environmental Program, the United Nations
Convention on the Law of the Sea, and the Disarmament and International Security Committee — indicating a
substantive, research-driven program rather than a casual interest club. [Source: charlottecountryday.org school news
— Middle School MUN]
STEM and other academic clubs
Robotics is confirmed by name through student profiles in the school's news archive, where students cite robotics as a
primary activity. No public competition results (FIRST, VEX, or similar) surfaced for the Upper School robotics program.
[Source: charlottecountryday.org school news — scholarship nominee profiles]
Gap note: Several academic-competition clubs common at peer schools — Science Olympiad, quiz/knowledge bowl,
debate, and DECA — could not be confirmed for Charlotte Country Day in public sources. Their absence here means
“not found,” not “does not exist.” This is the kind of named-club detail held in the login-gated activities catalog. The
audio script will not assert these programs exist.
Compiled June 26, 2026. Sources cited inline and listed at end of each document. Page 1

The affinity groups operate under the Diversity Awareness Forum (DAF), which the school describes as the umbrella
community bringing the groups' voices together. A Diversity Awareness Lunch Forum, established in 2014, offers
students and faculty a recurring setting for discussion. All incoming Upper School students are introduced to DAF
through a required Freshman Seminar. [Source: charlottecountryday.org DEIB Our Program]
Leadership development
The Student Diversity Leadership Corps (SDLC) gives selected Upper School students a leadership role supporting the
school's diversity planning. Country Day also sends students to the National Association of Independent Schools (NAIS)
Student Diversity Leadership Conference and hosts/participates in an Affirming Community Together (ACT) conference.
[Source: charlottecountryday.org DEIB Our Program]
Other divisions and parent groups
Beyond the Upper School, the Middle School runs five affinity groups (an African American Affinity Group, a Jewish
Culture Club, MOSAIC, a Multiracial Affinity Group, and a South Asian Affinity Group), and the Lower School runs a
Students of Color Affinity Group for grades 1–4. Parent affinity communities include POCIS and an International Parents
Group. [Source: charlottecountryday.org DEIB Our Program]

Overview
Charlotte Country Day School is a JK–12 independent, nonsectarian college-preparatory school founded in 1941 and
serving roughly 1,700 students across two campuses (Cannon and Bissell). Its Upper School describes a robust
co-curricular program built on student-led organizations spanning service, special-interest, and affinity clubs,
complemented by signature traditions. [Sources: charlottecountryday.org Upper School page; charlottecountryday.org

students may “join student-led organizations that include nearly 50 clubs,” while the 2025–26 School Profile lists “45

Brothers Big Sisters, and more.” We report the range (about 45–50) rather than asserting a single figure. [Sources:

Honor Code and Honor Council
The Honor Code anchors Country Day's student-governance culture. Students sign the code each year and write the
Honor Pledge — “I will not lie, cheat, or steal, nor will I tolerate those who do” — on graded work. Violations such as
lying, cheating, and plagiarism trigger an Honor Council hearing in Middle and Upper School, with disciplinary and
academic consequences. The Honor Council is thus both a student-leadership body and the school's primary
integrity-enforcement mechanism. [Sources: charlottecountryday.org CD Education; charlottecountryday.org BucsNet
Quick Reference; Axios Charlotte sponsored feature]
Student Government and student leadership
Student Government appears consistently in the school's club listings and Upper School materials as a core leadership
organization, where students participate in governance, assist peers, and serve as role models. The Student Diversity
Leadership Corps (SDLC) provides a parallel, inclusion-focused leadership track. [Sources: charlottecountryday.org
School Profile; charlottecountryday.org Upper School page; charlottecountryday.org DEIB Our Program]
Club chartering and funding (folded-in topic)
Gap note: Per the series convention, the Funding & Discovery topic is folded into Governance here because the
underlying data is thin. Country Day does not publicly document how Upper School clubs are proposed, chartered,
advised, or funded — those mechanics typically live in the student handbook and the BucsNet/Veracross portal. We
therefore confirm the governance bodies (Honor Council, Student Government, SDLC) but cannot detail the
club-chartering or budgeting process. The audio script will reflect this limitation.
Sources

# NotebookLM Prompt — Inside Charlotte Country Day: Clubs & Activities

_Paste everything below the line into NotebookLM as the episode prompt. Character count of the pasteable body: 4950 (within the 4,990 ceiling)._

---

You are producing one episode of a school-activities podcast titled "Inside Charlotte Country Day: Clubs & Activities." Two hosts, conversational and balanced. Base every claim on the attached dossiers; do not invent clubs, names, or results. Never use "elite," "powerhouse," or "dynasty." Do not name individual students or advisors. Bracketed cues are source hints — read them silently, never aloud.

REQUIRED COVERAGE: deliver all eight segments below AND the closing disclaimer — don't drop or rush later ones. If time runs short, trim early banter and analogies first, never later substance or the closing.

Open by having a host lay out the full agenda in plain language — naming all eight segment topics below, in order. Then note naturally: Country Day's sports teams and its arts, theatre, and music programs are NOT covered here — each already got its own dedicated episode earlier in this series.

Segment 1 — Club program overview. Country Day offers roughly 45 to 50 student-led Upper School clubs; the figure varies across the school's own materials, so say "about 45 to 50." Be honest that a complete public club roster isn't published — this episode covers clubs confirmed in public sources, not every club that exists. [Catalog dossier]

Segment 2 — Affinity & identity groups, the strongest area. Nine DISTINCT Upper School affinity groups, all open to all students, sit under the Diversity Awareness Forum: Amigos (written "Amig@s"), the Asian Affinity Club, the Black Student Union, the Interfaith Club, the International Club, the Jewish Culture Club, Multi (a standalone multiracial-identity group — keep it separate; do not fold "Multi" or the word "multiracial" into the Jewish Culture Club or any other group), PRISSM, and SWAG. The school's Upper School page advertises "seven" while its DEIB page lists nine — mention both honestly rather than picking one. Note the umbrella: the Diversity Awareness Forum coordinates the groups, a 2014 Lunch Forum hosts dialogue, all freshmen meet it via a required seminar, and the Student Diversity Leadership Corps plus the N-A-I-S conference add a leadership track. [Affinity dossier]

Segment 3 — Academic & competition clubs. Model UN is the flagship: at U-N-C Chapel Hill's MUNCH conference in March 2025, seventeen students competed and six earned awards — four of them Outstanding Delegate. The program also took a Best Delegate award and a commendation at a Virginia conference and has competed at a Duke-hosted event. Robotics is confirmed by name but has no public competition results. Then say plainly: Science Olympiad, debate, quiz bowl, and DECA could not be confirmed — that means "not found in public sources," not "doesn't exist." [Academic dossier]

Segment 4 — Service & civic engagement. Big Brothers Big Sisters draws about half of juniors and seniors into weekly mentoring at Rama Road Elementary; the whole Upper School staffs the Special Olympics Spring Games every April since 1984; and a Senior Externship connects seniors with 175-plus employers. [Service dossier]

Segment 5 — Honor societies. Five recognition societies: National Honor Society, National Junior Honor Society, National Art Honor Society, Tri-M Music Honor Society, and the Cum Laude Society. Frame these as selective recognition, not open-enrollment clubs; do not invent specific induction criteria (GPA cutoffs, portfolio rules) — those aren't documented. [Honor societies dossier]

Segment 6 — Governance & leadership. The Honor Code anchors student life — students sign it yearly and write the pledge "I will not lie, cheat, or steal, nor will I tolerate those who do" on graded work, with an Honor Council hearing violations. Student Government leads student life. Note honestly that how clubs are chartered and funded isn't publicly documented. [Governance dossier]

Segment 7 — Publications & media; be candid this is thin. Perspectives is a school magazine, not a student club; the yearbook was historically "Postscript"; no student newspaper or literary magazine could be confirmed. Don't imply more than the evidence shows. [Publications dossier]

Segment 8 — Signature achievements. Recap Model UN's documented awards, then two institutional strengths: the nine-group affinity ecosystem and service at scale. [Signature dossier]

Close with takeaways, then deliver this disclaimer sincerely: we apologize if we missed any club or activity — we're reporting only what our research surfaced, and Country Day's full catalog isn't entirely public.

Pronunciation: "Model U-N"; "MUNCH" as one word; "I-B" and "International Baccalaureate"; "D-A-F"; "PRISSM" like prism; "SWAG"; "S-D-L-C"; "Amig@s" is the single word Amigos (ah-MEE-gohs) — the "@" is a stylized letter A; never voice the symbol, never read it as "at," and never expand the name into separate words (e.g., not "Ahead of Me Goes"); "Rama Road" = RAH-mah Road (not "Ramroat"); "Tri-M" = try-em; "Cum Laude" = koom-LAU-day.

Big Brothers Big Sisters
Country Day's chapter of Big Brothers Big Sisters is among its most prominent service organizations. A sponsored
feature reports that nearly half of the junior and senior classes mentor students at Rama Road Elementary on a weekly
basis, forming sustained mentoring relationships. [Source: Axios Charlotte sponsored feature, Oct. 2024]
Special Olympics Spring Games
Each April the entire Upper School — students, faculty, and staff — pauses academics for two days to host the Special
Olympics Mecklenburg County Spring Games, with students serving as buddies, timekeepers, and event assistants.
The school's history timeline dates this tradition on the Cannon Campus to 1984, making it one of Country Day's
longest-running service commitments. [Sources: charlottecountryday.org Beyond the Classroom;
charlottecountryday.org Our History]
Senior Externship Program
During senior year, students complete the Senior Externship Program, a one-day job-shadowing and mentoring
experience connecting their interests to working professionals. The school reports the program has partnered with more
than 175 area employers across 20-plus industries since its 2017 launch, many of them Country Day parents and
alumni. [Source: charlottecountryday.org Beyond the Classroom]
Student-driven service affiliations
Student profiles in the school's news archive reference additional service involvement — for example, volunteering with
Charlotte Sister Cities and RunningWorks — illustrating the breadth of civic engagement, though these reflect individual
students' activities rather than confirmed standalone clubs. [Source: charlottecountryday.org school news — student
profiles]

Documented club achievements
Country Day's clearest, source-backed club achievements come from Model UN, whose delegations earned a Best
Delegate award and verbal commendation at a Virginia conference and six awards — including four Outstanding
Delegate honors — at the MUNCH conference in March 2025, with additional success at a Duke-hosted conference.
Taken together these results mark Model UN as the program's flagship competitive club. [Sources:
charlottecountryday.org school news — MUNCH, Virginia, and Duke MUN posts]
Signature institutional strengths
Two non-competition strengths stand out. First, the affinity-and-inclusion ecosystem: nine Upper School affinity groups
coordinated under the Diversity Awareness Forum, supported by a Student Diversity Leadership Corps and
national-conference participation — a more developed structure than many peer schools publish. Second, service at
scale: the entire Upper School staffs the Special Olympics Spring Games each April (a tradition since 1984), and
roughly half of the junior and senior classes mentor weekly through Big Brothers Big Sisters. [Sources:
charlottecountryday.org DEIB Our Program; charlottecountryday.org Beyond the Classroom; Axios Charlotte sponsored
feature]
Claims excluded from this dossier
Gap note: A third-party school-review site characterizes Country Day's theatre program as having “state titles.” Two
reasons keep it out of this clubs dossier: (1) theatre/arts is covered in a previously released dedicated episode in this
series, and (2) the claim is not corroborated by a primary source. Including it would risk both cross-episode duplication
and an unverified superlative. The audio script avoids the terms “elite,” “powerhouse,” and “dynasty” throughout, since
the sourced data supports specific accomplishments rather than blanket superlatives.
